Codex Security scans repositories, reviews changes, tracks findings over time and runs checks in CI, requiring Node 22+ and Python 3.10+, with either a ChatGPT sign-in or an API key for authentication (HN discussion). It is Apache-2.0 licensed and one of the people working on it says it was open-sourced early and will change quickly.

  • Several commenters report hitting refusal errors during scans and want clarity on which projects are in scope and how ownership of the code is determined.
  • One reading is that this is mainly a convenient CI wrapper around existing models; others point to comparable tools including an open-source scanner with a large following and a recently open-sourced Alibaba code-review CLI.

The Model Context Protocol spec dropped sessions and the initialize handshake. The 2026-07-28 release makes every request self-describing, retires the Mcp-Session-Id header, moves method and tool names into HTTP headers for gateway routing, adds cache hints to list responses, and replaces held-open server-initiated streams with Multi Round-Trip Requests (HN discussion). Authorization changes include RFC 9207 issuer validation and a shift away from Dynamic Client Registration, alongside a twelve-month deprecation policy.

  • Commenters running long workflows — some lasting days — ask what replaces the persistent connection they were depending on.
  • Others who already moved to stateless HTTP report better reliability but note reconnection and timeout rough edges in practice, and one suggests URL paths could carry the routing information now placed in headers.

uv shipped its first breaking release since March. Version 0.12.0 makes uv init declare a build system and use a packaged src/ layout by default, and rejects legacy source-distribution formats such as .tar.bz2 and .tar.xz along with wheels containing bzip2, LZMA or XZ-compressed entries (HN discussion). Existing projects are unaffected, and the maintainers expect most users to upgrade without changes.

  • A maintainer is answering questions in the thread, including on supply-chain safety around exclude-newer and how to handle unpinned git dependencies.
  • Recurring requests include a sensible uv upgrade for bumping all dependencies and better output from the show commands.

A research project runs a 2.8-trillion-parameter model on a 64 GB laptop chip, very slowly. Deltafin executes Kimi K3 by keeping the resident model on MPS, CUDA or CPU and streaming routed MXFP4 experts, with a reference figure of 0.0687 tokens per second — about 14.6 seconds per token — on an M1 Max (HN discussion). Each token reads roughly 25.8 GB of expert data, which is why the full local mode wants about 1.7 TB of disk and the streaming mode is minutes per token.

  • Commenters question whether that throughput counts as usable at all, given a thousand tokens would take most of a day.
  • Others raise SSD wear as the real constraint, since the design reads tens of gigabytes per token, and point to reports of faster streaming on newer Apple hardware or across multiple large-memory machines.

Andrew Ng announced a new AI education company backed by Coursera. LearnVector is a Mountain View company founded in 2026 with a $100 million investment from Coursera, building agentic systems intended to plan a learning path, adapt to the learner and stay with them until a skill is mastered (HN discussion). The site says the team is hiring and expects to show products by early 2027.

  • Several commenters note edtech's historically weak venture returns and argue the Coursera relationship, with its existing content library, is the main thing that could offset that.
  • Others push back on the "one-to-one" framing since the tutor is a model rather than a person, and note that simple Socratic-method prompts already work reasonably well, while questioning whether current models are tuned for teaching rather than answering.

A long post surveys SQLite tuning for server-side use. The article walks through WAL mode, the four checkpointing strategies, synchronous = NORMAL, busy timeouts, and the single-writer constraint that produces SQLITE_BUSY (HN discussion). Its central argument is that on local NVMe, eliminating network round-trips matters more than the features a client-server database adds.

  • Practitioners suggest serialising writes through a single application-level writer rather than relying on busy timeouts, and caution that synchronous = NORMAL trades away durability for recent transactions.
  • Some suspect the piece is model-generated and note it skips the operational annoyances that bite before performance tuning does, including how to attach a GUI client to a database file living on the app server.

Someone spent three weeks testing multiple mice and keyboards on one Wayland desktop. The write-up finds the core Wayland protocol has deep multi-seat support — every input event ties to a seat — and rates compositors and toolkits individually, with sway and River strong, Weston and SDL middling, and niri having no support yet (HN discussion). The author published patched libraries and small tools alongside the post and flagged open project ideas.

  • Commenters point out that toolkits and applications assume a single focused window, so APIs like GTK's active-window and Qt's equivalent break down under multiple seats.
  • A compositor author says supporting this properly is considerably more work than it appears, and others note adjacent cases that already stress the assumption, such as laptops with both a touchscreen and a pointer, or eye tracking in mixed reality.

Scripps researchers argue ocean and freshwater oxygen loss should be treated as a critical planetary process. A Scripps-led review calls for aquatic deoxygenation to be formally recognised among the processes under threat (HN discussion). The framing centres on changes that would be irreversible on human timescales.

  • Commenters note the link is a university press release and point to the underlying peer-reviewed paper for the actual findings.
  • Several add context that oxygen loss and coastal dead zones already occur; the shift the review describes is in how widespread and persistent they become, with some effects potentially lasting centuries.

Half-Life now runs on PowerPC Macs under Mac OS 9. A developer using a fork of Xash3D FWGS, a re-implementation of the GoldSrc engine, produced a port that is playable start to finish with multiplayer, plus Blue Shift and Opposing Force, on G3 and G4 machines running OS 9.0 or later (HN discussion). Valve had planned a Mac OS 9 release in 1999 but cancelled it before launch, and did not ship a Mac version until 2013 on Intel.

  • For some readers the more interesting discovery is Xash3D FWGS itself — an open-source GoldSrc re-implementation that has existed since around 2011 and that many had not encountered.
  • Commenters note the target hardware is roughly period-correct for the 1998–99 iMacs, with VRAM the practical limit on playability.
  • The developer has said publicly that AI tooling assisted the work, which still took well over 40 hours spread across a couple of months.

An illustrated tour of the tools the demo scene built for itself. The piece catalogues Amiga-era sine-table precalculators, Seka and AsmOne assemblers, memory rippers for extracting music and graphics after a crash, and the tracker lineage from Ultimate Soundtracker through NoiseTracker to ProTracker (HN discussion). Many interfaces prioritised looking impressive over being legible.

  • A former Amiga scene coder says they generated sine tables from their own code and had no idea dedicated precalc tools existed at the time.
  • One commenter offers an explanation for the recurring "sinus" spelling: many sceners came from European language backgrounds that retained the Latin form rather than English's "sine".

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — July 28, 2026
item.description:
A quieter Tuesday: open-weights policy, a batch of model releases and benchmarks, and a handful of durable engineering and human-factors stories.

Anthropic's CEO published a position statement on open-weights models. Dario Amodei writes that Anthropic has never advocated banning open-weights models, calls those without dangerous capabilities a public good, and argues that barring US companies from using Chinese open models would not address his actual concerns — since bad actors are unlikely to be legitimate US businesses (the post, HN discussion). Instead he supports chip export restrictions, deterring industrial-scale distillation, and mandatory pre-release safety testing for all sufficiently capable models regardless of origin.

  • Several commenters read the anti-distillation plank as self-serving — a company that trained on the open web now seeking to restrict a cheaper path for competitors.
  • Others question the framing that some models are simply free of dangerous capabilities, asking where that line would actually be drawn; a minority find the stated risk argument reasonable on its merits.

An independent run of Claude models on SlopCodeBench found modest gains. The author benchmarked Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 on a 17-checkpoint subset of SlopCodeBench, a March 2026 benchmark from UW Madison that reveals requirements incrementally rather than up front (write-up, HN discussion). Opus 5 scored 24% strict pass against Opus 4.6's 17% in the original paper, and all models showed rising verbosity and code-smell metrics over a challenge, with Opus 5 writing roughly five times as many functions as Opus 4.8.

  • Commenters ask how much of the degradation is a harness and system-prompt problem rather than a model one, suggesting instructions to minimize blast radius and clean up after each task.
  • Reactions to Opus 5 itself are split — some report it as a solid efficiency win over 4.8 at lower token cost, others find it overconfident and verbose and have gone back to earlier models.

Moonshot AI released open weights for Kimi K3, and inference providers began hosting it. Telnyx's release note describes a 2.8-trillion-parameter model with a 1M-token context window, native vision, configurable reasoning effort and tool calling, priced at $2.70 per million input tokens and $13.50 per million output (release notes, HN discussion). The company says it serves the model on GPUs it owns and operates, which it argues is necessary for a model of that size.

  • Commenters push back on the claim that owning the hardware means pricing reflects cost rather than margin, and ask the provider to state its markup directly.
  • Others immediately posted comparable listings from other providers at near-identical per-token prices, noting the differences come down to cache pricing.

An engineer wrote about pointing a coding agent at a self-hosted open model. The author got opencode running against a Kimi K3 endpoint on Modal, where they work, in about five minutes, and describes the appeal as ownership of the endpoint and a shorter data path rather than raw capability (post, HN discussion). The motivation was practical: not wanting to upgrade a personal Claude plan for a side project.

  • Multiple commenters note the author's employer disclosure and question whether leased GPU capacity really counts as your own infrastructure.
  • The most-requested missing detail is cost — commenters point out frontier APIs are widely believed to be subsidized, so a private endpoint could land either side of them, and that number is what would make the comparison useful.

A consultancy reported that a $500 reinforcement-learning fine-tune of a 9B open model outperformed frontier configurations on a catalog-review task. The GRPO-trained model reached 87.3% of the maximum achievable score versus 76.9% for the best frontier setup and 64.2% for its own untrained base, at $0.50 per 1,000 listings (article, HN discussion). The piece frames this within a broader argument about workflow redesign and measurement being the differentiators in AI adoption.

  • Commenters ask how the scorer grades each episode — if a frontier model assigns the grade, it is unclear how the ceiling holds once the tuned model surpasses it.
  • The cited Ramp revenue correlation draws a post-hoc objection: companies already growing have money to spend on AI, which would produce the same chart.
  • Several note that narrow task-specific wins don't transfer, and that a specialist beating generalists on one vaguely defined benchmark says little about general capability.

Fermion Research published Neutrino-1 8B, an 8.19B-parameter model in a ternary-family weight format. The model ships as a single 3.88 GB container that decodes bit-packed weights inside the matrix kernels, with only the 252 transformer linears using the coded format while embeddings stay int8; reported figures include 72.1 on MMLU and 763 tok/s with speculative decoding on an H100 (model page, HN discussion). It is derived from Apache-2.0 Qwen3-8B and distributes through pip, a GGUF pack with a llama.cpp fork, and MLX.

  • Commenters point to prior art — the BitNet b1.58 paper and a competing ternary conversion of the same Qwen base at a smaller footprint — and question how proprietary the method really is.
  • Several object to the single-container distribution model, arguing that llama.cpp's modularity is a large part of why local inference improved, and that opaque artifacts work against that.

A 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Japan. The Japan Meteorological Agency posted event details and shaking intensity by prefecture and municipality (JMA page, HN discussion).

  • Commenters note the magnitude and location resemble the 2016 Kumamoto earthquakes, and that major cities appear to have avoided the highest intensities.

A Canadian man served 18 months in prison after police missed a single underscore in an identifier. Ars Technica reports the transcription error led to charges including luring and possession of child sexual abuse material, and the conviction was later voided (article, HN discussion).

  • Commenters quoting the piece highlight that nothing else linked the accused to the complainant — no images were found and investigators could not show he had accessed the messaging service during the relevant period — and ask what evidence supported the conviction.
  • Others note the article does not say whether any compensation followed, given the served sentence, lost income and lasting reputational damage.

python-build-standalone produces self-contained, portable CPython distributions. The project builds full-featured Python installations that statically link or bundle their library dependencies and limit the CPU instructions used, aiming to run on any system for a target architecture; some builds ship object files and metadata so downstream repackagers can strip features like SQLite or OpenSSL (documentation, HN discussion).

  • Commenters note maintenance moved to Astral and that these are the distributions uv installs, as do pipx, Hatch, Poetry and Bazel; maintainer-side comments describe the ongoing work as tracking upstream CPython and upstreaming changes where possible.
  • Practical caveats raised: portability boundaries still show up at glibc version, CPU feature level and third-party native extensions, and musl builds that drop libc dependencies cannot load ordinary .so extensions.
  • Cosmopolitan/APE is offered as an alternative approach, shipping a roughly 40 MB Python binary that runs across several operating systems from one file.

Apple's Vehicle Motion Cues feature displays animated dots that track vehicle movement to reduce motion sickness. The iPhone accessibility setting can be enabled manually or via automatic detection while riding in a vehicle (Apple support page, HN discussion).

  • Commenters report it working well in practice for passengers who otherwise cannot look at a screen in a car, and note the same capability exists on MacBooks.
  • An open-source Android equivalent is available on F-Droid for people outside the Apple ecosystem.

A history professor embedded white-text instructions in an online assignment prompt to detect AI use. The hidden text told a chatbot to insert nonsensical references to Madagascar into an essay about the Industrial Revolution; 32 of 35 students across two classes submitted answers containing phrases like "Madagascar purple bicycle whispers to the ceiling" and failed that portion (article, HN discussion). Students were given the opportunity to contest the grade, and two did.

  • Commenters note the assessment appears to have been an online discussion post rather than a proctored midterm, which affects how the numbers should be read.
  • Several raise selection bias: stories reporting dramatic detection rates circulate widely, while attempts finding low rates would not, and anyone editing the output would have removed the tell entirely.

An essay profiles Michiyo Yasuda, the color designer behind Studio Ghibli's palettes. Yasuda defined the cel colors for most of the studio's output from Castle in the Sky onward — over 300 colors on that first film — mixing custom paints in muted intermediate shades at a time when the industry favored bright, flat ones, and adapting her process when Ghibli moved to digital coloring (article, HN discussion). Takahata described her as choosing texture rather than color, citing faded trousers in Grave of the Fireflies.

  • Commenters single out the article's side-by-side of a standard versus Yasuda's final color design for Kiki as the clearest demonstration of what the role actually contributes.
  • One raises a succession question — whether Ghibli developed anyone to carry the craft forward, or whether apprentices simply dispersed to other studios as the studio wound down.

DConf 2026 will run September 2–4 in London, with livestreams for remote attendees. The D Programming Language Conference returns with talks from Walter Bright and Vladimir Panteleev among others, and the published first-day schedule leans heavily on LLM topics, including a session on integrating LLMs into Phobos 3 development and the rules established for their use (conference site, HN discussion).

  • Commenters question the LLM emphasis for a standard-library rewrite, arguing Phobos 3 would benefit more from betterC-friendly containers and closer alignment with C++ move and copy semantics.
  • One thread asks about the status of the OpenD fork and whether it has had any effect beyond diverting an upstream contributor.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — July 27, 2026
item.description:
A quieter-than-usual Saturday list: one legal test of privacy tooling, a very large open model due today, and several careful engineering projects.

US prosecutors charge an Atlanta man after his GrapheneOS phone wiped itself during an airport search. The Department of Justice is using a federal statute against destroying property to prevent its seizure, after a device running the privacy-focused Android variant erased itself when a passcode was entered during secondary screening at Hartsfield-Jackson in January of last year (TechSpot, HN discussion). Security researchers quoted in the piece say they have not seen the law applied to an operating system before; a ruling on the defense's motion to suppress is not expected before late October.

  • Commenters point to VeraCrypt's hidden-volume design, where a decoy password unlocks a plausible-looking system, as older prior art that may be more defensible than a duress PIN that visibly destroys data.
  • Several note the evidentiary problem: past encrypted-device cases have generally required substantial independent proof that incriminating material existed before an inference from its destruction was allowed.

An interactive visual model of the PostgreSQL engine, styled as a city, was published as an early prototype. PGSimCity animates how the database's internal components interact, and its author labels it explicitly as unreviewed and likely to contain inaccuracies in both the model and explanations (PGSimCity, HN discussion).

  • Readers broadly liked the format but said the guided tour presents too much at once and covers too much screen; multiple asked for interactive stepping rather than passive auto-advancing.
  • A common wish was to submit a query and follow it end to end, from parsing through execution to output, alongside the background processes that run independently.

Moonshot AI has scheduled the open-weights release of Kimi-K3 for July 27. The Hugging Face page describes a 3-trillion-parameter-class model with a new attention architecture, native tool calling and browsing, and a context window aimed at repository-scale code (Hugging Face, HN discussion). At the time of posting the weights were still behind a countdown rather than public.

  • One commenter estimates roughly 1.5TB of VRAM to host it natively at mxfp4, putting it at the edge of an 8-GPU node and effectively out of reach for local use, with third-party pricing likely to serve as the first real datapoint on what serving a model this size costs.

Seasonal forecast models now give roughly a 90% chance of a record-setting El Niño. Across 667 ensemble members from 14 models, the July runs put the median peak Niño 3.4 anomaly at about 3.6C, against a prior record of 2.75C in 2015-16, with the middle 80% of members at or above that old record (The Climate Brink, HN discussion). Successive monthly runs since March have each revised warmer, and the author notes model agreement is not the same as skill.

  • Commenters highlight a point easy to miss in the charts: global temperature lags ENSO by several months, so most of the warming from this event would land in 2027 rather than this year.
  • Several observe that the models kept underestimating observed ocean temperatures, and that regional consequences — rainfall versus heat in a given city — remain hard to read from the index alone.

Vercel Labs released scriptc, a compiler that turns TypeScript into native binaries without embedding a JavaScript engine. The project type-checks with the real TypeScript compiler and compiles supported constructs to native code, reporting a per-statement coverage figure and rejecting anything it cannot compile with a specific error code rather than silently miscompiling; an optional mode links in quickjs-ng for dynamic code (GitHub, HN discussion).

  • Commenters raise the ecosystem problem: most npm packages ship untyped JavaScript with separate declaration files, so real projects would still need the dynamic engine, and greenfield code without dependencies could already use AssemblyScript.
  • Others point to porffor as a longer-running attempt at the same goal that passes roughly 68% of Test262, and express skepticism about how quickly this project claims to have gotten further.

A writeup argues that LLMs make dependently-typed languages practical by automating proof effort. The author built a Zstandard decompressor in Lean, citing the seL4 retrospective — about ten times as much time on proofs as on design and implementation, and over twenty times as many lines of proof as C — as the historical barrier, and notes that because only a proof's existence matters, generated proofs need not be elegant (ImperialViolet, HN discussion).

  • Commenters agree cost was the main obstacle but flag a remaining alignment problem: without human review, machine-generated proofs can drift from the intended specification, and contract-style Hoare or separation logic is easier to keep legible.
  • One notes that verified assembly is less speculative than the article's closing suggests, pointing to existing Fiat Crypto and CryptOpt work already used for cryptographic routines.

A small project reproduces the sound of specific cassette tapes using ffmpeg filter chains. Each profile applies tape hiss, wow and flutter pitch modulation, bandwidth limits and EQ, with presets for stocks including BASF LH Extra C90, Maxell UD C90, two 1978 Sony CHF tapes, a late-era TDK D90, and the Soviet MK-60 (GitHub, HN discussion).

  • One commenter objects on technical grounds that wow and flutter come from the transport mechanism of the deck playing the tape, not from the tape stock itself.
  • Others ask how the per-tape parameters were derived — by ear or by measurement against reference recordings — and whether neural amp modeling tools would capture the character better.

A researcher reports that malware-hosting repositories remain easy to find on GitHub via ordinary search. The author describes a recurring pattern — README files with an emoji "Download" heading linking to a versioned zip archive on githubusercontent.com — and says that after a previous article led GitHub to delete the 10,000 repositories a script had identified, newly created ones went unblocked for a month (Orchid Files, HN discussion).

  • Several commenters attribute the pattern to under-resourcing rather than incompetence, noting that security functions are cost centers that tend to get funded only after revenue pressure.
  • Others caution that systematic policing of public repos becomes an arms race with false positives, which is part of why platforms prefer reactive takedowns of specific lists.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — July 26, 2026
item.description:
A quiet Sunday's worth of technology news: smaller models doing more, institutions writing rules for AI, and several long-running hardware bets asking for patience.

Anthropic says it cut most of Claude Code's system prompt for its newest models. In a post on context engineering, the company reports removing over 80% of Claude Code's system prompt for Claude Opus 5 and Fable 5 with no measurable loss on its coding evaluations, arguing that rigid rules in system prompts, skills and CLAUDE.md files now conflict with each other more than they help. The recommended shift is from explicit prohibitions toward letting the model use judgement, with a /doctor command to trim existing configuration (HN discussion).

  • Several commenters say this is unsurprising in practice — they have long found that fighting a model's default behaviours with instructions works worse than editing the output afterwards.
  • One reader is skeptical of the framing, reading it as moving tuning out of portable Markdown files into Anthropic-specific tooling, and reports more accidental deletions and higher token use with Opus 5 than with 4.8.

Debian is voting on whether to restrict LLM-assisted contributions. A General Resolution now in its discussion period puts four proposals to the project; Proposal A would forbid contributions written with the use or assistance of LLMs across source packages, official project software, web resources, documentation, translations and official communication, while explicitly excluding upstream projects, AI-related software and upstream patches. Its stated rationale is the unclear copyright status of model output against Debian Policy and DFSG licensing requirements (HN discussion).

  • Much of the thread turns on the undefined word "assistance" — whether using a model as a search interface, or having it locate a bug that a human then fixes by hand, would fall inside the ban.
  • Commenters also question the proposal's description of LLMs as producing merely likely combinations of training data, and wonder how much existing documentation and translation work would already be non-compliant.

A leaked transcript of a DeepSeek investor meeting circulated alongside news that the company paused a funding round. The translated PDF attributes remarks to founder Liang Wenfeng framing the gap with US labs as one of compute resources rather than people, and saying the company cannot afford to train models at the largest current scale (HN discussion).

  • Commenters point to reporting that the pause followed the remarks circulating widely online, and warn the headline is easy to misread as the pause being caused by the compute gap itself.
  • Readers who worked through the transcript describe the tone as notably more measured than public statements from US lab leaders.

A Stanford policy brief finds little evidence so far of AI-driven job losses. The SIEPR summary reports that unemployment among the most AI-exposed quintile of workers rose 0.77 percentage points since 2022 versus 0.85 points for the least exposed, that software developer job postings have grown faster than average over the past year, and that firms adopting enterprise AI saw employment grow. It allows that the weak market for recent graduates may be partly attributable to AI, and that early evidence is not the last word (HN discussion).

  • A recurring caveat is timing: commenters argue coding and general-purpose agents only became broadly useful very recently, so studies drawing on 2022–2025 data may be measuring the chat era rather than the agent era.
  • Others note organisational inertia as a confounder, including large firms that still ban internal AI use, meaning low measured impact partly reflects low adoption.

Cloudflare is changing crawler defaults by traffic category. The announcement splits AI traffic into categories, blocking Training and Agent by default on ad-bearing pages for newly onboarded domains while leaving Search allowed, and from 15 September evaluating multi-purpose crawlers against all of their stated behaviours rather than their primary one (HN discussion).

  • Commenters flag the practical consequence for Googlebot, which serves both search indexing and Gemini training and would therefore fall under training blocks once the combined-behaviour rule applies.
  • Others note the scheme still depends on crawler self-declaration, and that pay-per-crawl remains behind a request-access form a year after being announced.

A 28.9-million-parameter language model runs locally on an $8 microcontroller. The project puts a 4-bit, 14.9 MB model on an ESP32-S3 with 512 KB of SRAM, generating about 9.5 tokens per second entirely on-device by keeping a 25-million-parameter embedding table in flash and reading roughly 450 bytes per token — an application of the Per-Layer Embeddings idea from Google's Gemma models. Trained on TinyStories, it writes short stories and cannot answer questions or follow instructions (HN discussion).

  • Commenters ask the obvious follow-up: whether the same flash-backed access pattern generalises to much larger models on ordinary CPUs.
  • One notes that usable text-to-speech models exist in the 20–30M parameter range, so a fully offline talking device on this class of chip looks plausible.

A 9.36M-parameter text-to-speech model was published with detailed evaluation numbers. Inflect-Micro-v2 is 37.53 MB in FP32, outputs 24 kHz mono, and runs at about 6.3× real time on four CPU threads; the author reports a 66.2% blind preference rate in a small community study and publishes per-recognizer word error rates alongside comparisons to KittenTTS, Piper and Supertonic (HN discussion).

  • Commenters clarify the headline's "complete voice" means text-to-speech only — not speech recognition — with one fixed English male voice and no zero-shot cloning.
  • Listeners split on quality: several call it remarkable for the size while describing the prosody as odd and comparable to older TTS systems.

GM is backing a US sodium-ion push for grid storage. IEEE Spectrum reports that Colorado-based Peak Energy, partnered with General Motors, is building a $71 million, 17,000-square-meter plant near Sacramento with 4 GWh of annual capacity, after Natron Energy and Bedrock Materials shut down their US sodium-ion operations last year. The company concedes it cannot match lithium-iron-phosphate on energy density or per-cell price, but claims 20% lower lifetime cost via passive cooling, with 20,000 cycles over 20 years to 80% capacity (HN discussion).

  • Commenters note the article's own detail that Peak sources its commercial cells from Chinese suppliers, making the near-term business assembly and sales rather than domestic cell manufacturing.
  • Someone operating LFP grid batteries says their sites draw half a megawatt to two megawatts continuously for HVAC, which makes the passive-cooling claim the most commercially interesting part.

JetZero is raising money and building factories for a blended-wing airliner. The company's site lists a roughly $175 million Series B led by B Capital, investments from United and Alaska Airlines with paths to future orders, a groundbreaking in Greensboro, North Carolina, and an LOI with EXIM Bank to explore up to $3 billion in financing, for a 250-seat all-wing Z4 it says uses up to 50% less fuel (HN discussion).

  • Aerospace-minded commenters list the structural reasons tube-and-wing dominates: pressurising a non-cylindrical hull, evacuation certification, and compatibility with existing jet bridges and ground equipment.
  • The windowless cabin with wraparound screens draws consistent doubt about passenger tolerance, separate from the question of whether a startup can certify an airliner at all.

Clinical trial failure rates have not improved across decades. A Science blog post examines long-run data showing roughly 91% of drug candidates entering clinical trials fail, and asks readers to imagine an equivalent rate in car or aircraft design (HN discussion).

  • Working researchers push back on the engineering comparison, arguing that mechanical design rests on well-characterised physics while biology offers no equivalent predictive base.
  • One commenter finds the flatness more surprising than the level, since picked-over low-hanging fruit should push failure rates up; another notes some "failed" trials contain drugs that work for identifiable patient subsets but are not pursued because the market is too narrow.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — July 25, 2026
item.description:
A quiet Saturday's worth of technology news: a proposed Android change with outsized downstream effects, two AI leaderboards, a database performance postmortem, a rocket test, and some marine biology.

A proposed Android change could restrict on-device ADB connections. A post from the developer of a Shizuku-based call recorder flags a comment by a Google ADB maintainer on a public IssueTracker thread suggesting that loopback ADB connections — where an Android device runs both the debug daemon and the client — may be restricted to limit abuse by bad actors. The author stresses this is not an official announcement, and notes that the change would affect Shizuku, libadb, and rootless privacy tools that rely on granting elevated permissions without a second machine (HN discussion).

  • Several commenters argue the recurring pattern is the absence of a configuration switch: they accept the security rationale but want the option to permit loopback ADB on their own hardware.
  • Others push back on the assumption that the device owner is the only person with physical access to an unlocked phone, pointing to border and institutional searches where such an attack could be automated; one view holds that on-device ADB is an architectural hack and the underlying capabilities should be exposed to apps directly instead.

Claude Opus 5 currently sits at the top of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. The leaderboard lists Opus 5 at its max and xhigh reasoning settings as the highest-scoring entries, ahead of Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, on a v4.1 index aggregating nine evaluations including Terminal-Bench, GPQA Diamond, Humanity's Last Exam, and an anti-hallucination measure (HN discussion).

  • Commenters direct attention to the intelligence-versus-cost view of the same data, noting the top model is among the most expensive listed while at least two others land within a couple of percentage points at roughly half the price.
  • Reported hands-on experience is mixed, with some describing worse debugging behaviour and over-building on tasks relative to earlier models, a reminder that a close aggregate ranking may not track individual workflows.

The ARC Prize leaderboards were also circulating. The ARC-AGI leaderboard spans three benchmark generations, with ARC-AGI-3 shifting from static puzzles to agents adapting on the fly to novel interactive environments, and plots cost-per-task against score; only systems costing under $10,000 per run are shown (HN discussion).

  • Some commenters raise the possibility that current models have simply absorbed ARC-style puzzles during training, and question why benchmark leaps have not translated into a lasting preference in their day-to-day work.
  • The cost axis draws its own scrutiny, with the highest per-task figures on the board compared unfavourably to what a human engineer would cost.

DBOS published a breakdown of why Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY bottlenecks, and how they got past it. Their engineering post traces a 2.9K writes/second ceiling — hit without saturating CPU, memory, or IOPS — to the global exclusive lock Postgres takes when committing a NOTIFY, which preserves commit-order delivery but serialises commits and defeats group commit; after optimisation they report 60K stream writes per second on a single server with millisecond latency (HN discussion).

  • One commenter notes the widely cited "doesn't scale" post the article responds to has carried a correction since May, and suggests the original claims were accurate for their time rather than made in bad faith.
  • A separate limitation raised is the roughly 8KB cap on notification payloads, which is fine when you can pass a row ID but awkward for transient events that never belong in a table; others ask how much of the speedup is available on stock Postgres versus tied to DBOS's own stack.

SpaceX flew Starship Flight 13. The mission page carried the livestream for the test flight (HN discussion).

  • Viewers in the thread report the booster's landing burn failed to light all engines and it went into the water, while the ship achieved a Raptor relight on orbit and a splashdown soft enough that it did not break up — with onboard cameras and the Starlink link reportedly still functioning afterwards.
  • Commenters treat the on-orbit relight as the milestone that matters, since it is the prerequisite for a flight that reaches orbit and deploys operational satellites.

Researchers described how sperm whales stay submerged while sleeping upright. A study from the University of St Andrews and Université de Neuchâtel, published in the Journal of Experimental Biology, used suction-cup tags recording sound and 3-D movement on whales off Norway to show that resting whales release gas bubbles to offset their natural positive buoyancy from spermaceti oil and expanding lung gas (announcement, HN discussion). The team also found that resting dives begin with less gas volume than deep foraging dives, and suspect a link to off-gassing of CO2 or N2.

  • A commenter points out the original paper's title is more precise than the press release: this is buoyancy regulation by modulating onboard gas volume, with bubble sounds used as the measurement, alongside modelling of tissue density and drag rather than "blowing bubbles" as a behaviour in itself.

Hannah Fry has won the 2026 Leelavati Prize for mathematics outreach. The Cambridge Faculty of Mathematics announcement notes the award, which recognises public communication of mathematics; Fry holds the Professorship of the Public Understanding of Mathematics there (HN discussion).

  • One commenter highlights that Fry was not admitted to Cambridge as an undergraduate mathematician and now holds a professorship at the institution.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — July 24, 2026
item.description:
A quieter-than-usual day, dominated by new multimodal AI models, a sobering gene-therapy story, and several reminders that convenience and reliability keep pulling in opposite directions.

Black Forest Labs announced FLUX 3, a multimodal foundation model. The early-access release jointly trains on images, video, and audio in one architecture and can generate video up to 20 seconds with native audio, with the company reporting preliminary win rates against several competing video generators (HN discussion). Open-weight access to the backbone is described as planned for the coming weeks and months rather than available now.

  • Commenters push back on the framing, questioning the "world model" language and noting the launch showed few human examples and used cuts rather than continuous 20-second takes.
  • Several read the marketing copy as LLM-generated and point out the open weights are near the bottom of the roadmap, not shipped.

The same FLUX 3 backbone is being used to control robots via a partnership with mimic. In a companion post, Black Forest Labs describes decoding robot actions from the video model's internal representation, with FLUX-mimic reportedly tested on production tasks at Audi (HN discussion). The claim is that a model trained hard on video prediction implicitly learns physical dynamics that transfer to manipulation.

  • Commenters note the underlying idea that good video models contain a world representation is not new, but flag it as notable for being a video lab moving into robotics.
  • One viewer points to a demo clip where the arm needed three attempts to reseat a window trim.

A girl who received an experimental gene-editing therapy in a Chinese trial died, and the death was not made public. Science reports the family paid over $800,000 for a never-before-tried brain-targeted therapy, per the investigation (HN discussion). The account raises questions about consent, risk disclosure, and payment in early human trials.

  • Commenters focus on risks appearing to be downplayed, including similar side effects reportedly seen earlier in monkey experiments.
  • Several highlight that the published paper drew an enthusiastic reception while reviewers were unaware a recipient had already died.

Google added a selfie video as a backup way to sign in to a Google Account. Users record guided head movements, and a later video is compared against it to confirm identity if locked out; Google says the video is encrypted and deletable (HN discussion). It is positioned as an optional recovery method.

  • Commenters are wary of handing Google more biometric data, framing it as another data-for-access trade.
  • Some contrast the cloud-based approach with Apple's local, on-device face recognition.

A long-time customer says Namecheap handed account access to an unverified third party. In a Tell HN post, the author describes an incoming club leader triggering a password reset on a domain registered to the author, followed by an unhelpful support response (HN discussion).

  • Multiple commenters report similar recent experiences, including abrupt profile-update-or-close-account threats and account lockouts.
  • Others note domain privacy protection would have hidden the email and blocked the reset, and mention Namecheap's recent private-equity acquisition.

A developer wrote about why software feels like it keeps getting worse despite better tooling. The essay catalogs everyday failures — flaky banking apps, buggy car infotainment — and argues stability rarely helps the KPIs teams are measured on (HN discussion).

  • Many commenters argue the decline predates AI and trace it to organizational misalignment and incentives that reward new features over reliability.

Someone launched Echo, a system that routes tasks across multiple open-weight models instead of one. The Show HN project claims frontier-level results at a fraction of the cost by picking the best model per problem from a pool including several open-weight models (HN discussion).

  • Commenters call it premature, noting no published benchmarks, no list of which models are used, a signup wall, and a privacy policy that permits training on inputs.
  • Others point to prior art, including reports that combining models can approach single-frontier-model performance and earlier router-style systems.

98.css, a CSS library that recreates the Windows 98 interface, resurfaced. The project styles semantic HTML into faithful late-90s controls with no JavaScript and works alongside any frontend framework (HN discussion).

  • Commenters note it recurs on HN every couple of years and list a broad ecosystem of similar retro UI kits mimicking Windows 95/XP/7 and other old systems.
